summary: Describes Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV), a control channel attached to a pseudowire along with operations such as connectivity checking. It works across the access circuit and transport types defined for pseudowires. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: VCCV lets the routers at the ends of a pseudowire send test messages through its forwarding path. The tests help an operator tell whether that path works and where a fault may be.

questions: how does vccv work over l2tpv3
how does vccv check a pseudowire
what are vccv control channel types
subtitle: How pseudowire endpoints negotiate and use a channel to check connectivity through the forwarding path.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire can appear established even when its forwarding path has a fault. Operators need an end-to-end way to check that path and diagnose failures.
tldr.mechanism: VCCV adds a control channel to a pseudowire. The two edge routers advertise supported channel and test types during setup, then exchange connectivity checks using the agreed types.
tldr.outcome: VCCV provides connectivity checks for MPLS and L2TPv3 pseudowires. RFC 5085 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 5586.

today: RFC 5085 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5586. Read the update with this specification.

sections.title: Why Pseudowires Need Connectivity Checks
sections.content:
A pseudowire emulates a service across a packet network. Customer devices see a link or circuit, while provider-edge (PE) routers carry the service between them. Operators need to check the pseudowire's actual forwarding state from one end to the other.

Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) provides a control channel between the pseudowire's ingress and egress points. It carries checks that help verify and diagnose the forwarding path. The document covers supported access-circuit and transport types for pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: Two PE routers carry a customer's service across a packet network. VCCV gives those routers a way to test whether traffic can cross the pseudowire between them.

sections.title: The Parts of VCCV
sections.content:
VCCV has three parts: signaling that tells a peer which capabilities are supported, an encapsulation that lets the receiving PE identify and intercept VCCV messages, and rules for the connectivity checks carried in those messages.

During pseudowire setup with LDP or L2TPv3, each side advertises the Control Channel (CC) and Connectivity Verification (CV) types it can receive. Once setup is complete, the PEs can send checks using compatible types. The encapsulation is designed to make a check follow the pseudowire's data path while keeping it from being forwarded to the customer edge.

An operator can run checks on a schedule or when needed. VCCV can also carry fault status, but mapping that status to native access technologies is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The two PE routers first announce which VCCV message formats they can handle. They can then send checks through the pseudowire, where the far PE recognizes them instead of sending them to the customer.

sections.title: Control Channel and Check Types
sections.content:
The CC type identifies how a VCCV message is carried. The CV type identifies the check inside it. A router may support multiple CV types, but only one CC type is used at a time. Both capability fields are 8-bit bitmasks.

For MPLS pseudowires, CC Type 1 uses the PW Associated Channel Header, Type 2 uses the MPLS Router Alert label, and Type 3 sets the pseudowire label's TTL to 1. MPLS CV types are ICMP Ping and MPLS LSP Ping. L2TPv3 defines one CC type, an L2-Specific Sublayer with its V-bit set, and ICMP Ping as its CV type.

The peers can use only types present in both advertisements. Once selected, a CC type stays in use until the pseudowire is signaled again. If no capability is advertised, the peer is treated as having no VCCV capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The channel type says how a check travels, and the check type says what message it carries. The routers can use only options both have announced, and keep the chosen channel until they set up the pseudowire again.

sections.title: VCCV over MPLS Pseudowires
sections.content:
MPLS VCCV messages travel over the same Label Switched Path as the pseudowire, either in-band or out-of-band. PE endpoints intercept them rather than forwarding them toward customer-edge devices. The three CC types provide different ways to identify the control message.

Type 1 uses a PW Associated Channel Header. Its first nibble is 0001, the Version and Reserved fields are zero, and the Channel Type is 0x0021 for IPv4 or 0x0057 for IPv6. It can be used only when the pseudowire uses the specified control-word format, and it must be supported when that control word is present.

Type 2 places the Router Alert label above the pseudowire label and works with or without a control word. Type 3 sets the pseudowire label TTL to 1. Both may take a different ECMP path from data traffic. ICMP Ping uses ICMPv4 or ICMPv6 according to the signaling addresses; LSP Ping follows RFC 4379 and identifies the pseudowire in its target FEC stack.
sections.plainLanguage: On MPLS, a check travels along the pseudowire and is intercepted by the far PE. The check must use a channel format and an IP version that match the pseudowire setup.

sections.title: VCCV over L2TPv3 Pseudowires
sections.content:
L2TPv3 Hello messages detect a dead peer or path for a group of sessions on a control connection. VCCV instead checks an individual L2TPv3 session, which gives a more specific view of that pseudowire's forwarding and signaling state.

The pseudowire must use an L2-Specific Sublayer that defines the V-bit. Setting this bit identifies the following message as VCCV. The message contains an ICMP Echo packet. Its source and destination addresses are the local and remote L2TP control-connection endpoint addresses, and its TTL or Hop Limit is 1.

The peers exchange a VCCV Capability AVP during session setup. An endpoint must not send VCCV messages until it has received the peer's capability. A request for the VCCV channel without a sublayer defining the V-bit requires the session to be disconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TPv3 VCCV checks one session at a time, while its Hello messages check a group of sessions. A V-bit marks the check, and the receiving endpoint uses the ICMP Echo packet to inspect that session.

sections.title: Congestion and Rate Limits
sections.content:
VCCV consumes bandwidth in addition to the bandwidth allocated for pseudowire data, so network planning must account for both. VCCV applications must consider congestion and describe how they manage bandwidth or packet frequency.

Outgoing checks should be rate-limited unless rate limiting could cause false connectivity failures. If the application cannot follow those limits, the RFC recommends an adaptive loss-based congestion-control scheme. ICMP and MPLS LSP Ping checks should use less than 5% of the pseudowire bit-rate.

Incoming checks may be policed to protect the router, but the policing should not be stricter than the bandwidth allocated to the VCCV channel. Otherwise, valid checks could be mistaken for a connectivity failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Checks use extra network capacity, so their rate needs a limit. The limit must still allow valid checks through, or the system could report a fault that is not there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VCCV adds security concerns in three areas: signaling of capabilities, the data channel, and the contents of the checks. The signaling extensions do not change the control-plane security rules in the cited LDP and L2TPv3 specifications.

An attacker or misconfigured device could inject, intercept, or flood VCCV messages. Floods can overload a peer or the path between a line card and a central processor. Implementations must provide a way to secure the data plane, such as IPsec for MPLS packets or a private MPLS network that prevents external packet injection. For L2TPv3, the Session ID separates traffic and a Cookie can add spoofing protection.

The security considerations for the ICMP and LSP Ping messages also apply to VCCV.
sections.plainLanguage: Forged or excessive checks can give false results or overload a router. The network needs data-plane protection and controls on how many checks it processes.
